name: The Elms

dates.altered: The survey records greenhouses and a service group built in 1911 on the Ida Powel Johnson estate Berwind acquired in 1909; the house passed to the Preservation Society of Newport County in 1962 and is a museum house.
dates.note: The style node's exemplar gives 1901 and the survey's own significance paragraph says 'completed in 1901'. Wikipedia gives 1901 for the infobox and 1909 as a date of subsequent work; the getarchive/PICRYL index of the same Library item prints 'Building/structure dates: 1901 Initial Construction' and a 1909 subsequent-work date. Nothing here disagrees, so nothing is reconciled.

quotes.text: B. Description of Exterior: 1. Over-all dimensions: 120 feet by 60 feet; rectangular, nine bays, 3 stories. 2. Foundations: The exterior walls are granite faced with brick on the interior. 3- Wall construction: The exterior walls are faced with limestone with a first floor coursing of granite. k. Structural system: The entire structure is framed in steel, with coffered brick arches in the first basement level.

quotes.text: 5. Chimneys: No chimney is visible above the blind balustrade which rings the roof line. Eleven low, rectangular chimneys, are .located on the third floor roof.
quotes.page: HABS No. RI-344, Part II.B.5; same extract span as the dimensions, no page marker legible

quotes.text: 6. Openings: a. Doorways: A three bay central projection on the east facade contains three arched doorways which are reached by a-^hort, low flight of six granite steps. The elaborate wrought iron and glass grillwork doors are framed by rusticated stonework with concave chamfering.
quotes.page: HABS No. RI-344, Part II.B.6.a; same extract span, no page marker legible

quotes.text: An eight foot high blind balus- trade conceals the third story, the servants quarters. This level is set back four to six feet from the balustrade. This service walk is tarred and gravelled. Slate shingles cover the inside wall of the balustrade and the exterior walls of the third story. Copper sheets are used as roofing of this story. Twelve metal ventilator shafts project through the walk and roof. Eight sculpture groups, installed in 1903, are located on the balustrade at the projecting corners of the bays and of the house proper.

note: Written for WP-11.2 Tranche 2, the French modes and the Beaux-Arts. Worth carrying to the kit layer: the survey states a 120 x 60 ft rectangle of nine bays in three storeys, an eight-foot blind balustrade hiding the third, and eleven chimneys none of which can be seen - a house whose chimney slot and whose parapet are doing the opposite of what a domestic revival kit assumes. AND ITS ROOF IS INVISIBLE, which matters because french-eclectic is the one node in this cluster whose identity is stated to rest 'almost entirely on roof geometry': the survey says a blind balustrade conceals the third storey, the slate is on the INSIDE wall of that balustrade and the roofing proper is copper sheet on a service walk. The academic French model this node carries has no visible roof at all. (An earlier draft of this note attributed to The Elms a phrase - 'Terra cotta rather than marble' - that belongs to beaux-arts-american's note on ROSECLIFF, a different building in the same town by a different architect. It was caught by re-reading the node file rather than the draft, and is recorded here because a misattributed quotation is the exact failure this directory exists to make impossible.)
